Yeah, so this is honestly one of the most uncertain parameters in the whole model, and we try to be upfront about that. The basic approach is to anchor on a few different lines of evidence and then put a fairly wide distribution over them rather than committing to a single point estimate.

One anchor is biological. The human brain is an existence proof that general intelligence capable of doing all the tasks in the economy is physically possible, so you can ask how much computation goes into producing a human-level mind. There's the compute the brain uses over a lifetime, roughly the training-run analog, and then there's what evolution spent searching over brain designs. Those give you very different numbers, a lifetime anchor is something like 10^24 FLOP while an evolutionary anchor is enormously larger, so they serve more as rough bounds than precise estimates.

The second line of evidence is empirical, looking at how capabilities have scaled with compute so far. We've watched successive orders of magnitude of training compute unlock new capabilities, and you can ask how many more orders of magnitude it seems to take to go from systems that do a handful of tasks well to systems that could do essentially every task a remote worker or a physical worker does. Part of that is thinking about the distribution of task difficulty across the economy. In GATE we model automation as gradual, so it's not a single threshold where everything flips. Each additional order of magnitude of effective compute automates some additional fraction of tasks, and full automation is the tail end of that.

And the "effective" part matters a lot. It's not just raw FLOP, it's FLOP adjusted for algorithmic progress. Algorithms have been improving at a pace that roughly matches or rivals hardware scaling, so the same physical compute gets you much more capability over time. So when we talk about the requirement for full automation, we mean effective compute measured in some base year's algorithmic units.

Where we ended up in the default settings is somewhere around 10^36 FLOP of effective compute for full automation, with a very wide uncertainty band, many orders of magnitude on either side. You could quite reasonably argue it's lower; some people think current paradigms are closer than that. You could argue it's higher if you think there are missing ingredients that scaling alone won't get you. The model is built so people can plug in their own views and see how sensitive the conclusions are, and one interesting result is that a lot of the qualitative dynamics, like the feedback loop where partial automation boosts investment in compute, which accelerates further automation, are fairly robust even as you vary this number quite a lot. What changes is mostly timing, not the overall shape of the trajectory.

r001.rationale: The response gives a default estimate of 10^36 FLOP and says uncertainty spans many orders of magnitude, but does not judge that the requirement is unlikely to be much greater than 10^40 FLOP.

r002.rationale: It identifies the computation evolution spent searching over brain designs as one benchmark for estimating the compute needed for a human-level mind.

r003.rationale: It does not compare evolution’s computational efficiency with current machine learning.

r004.rationale: It does not identify evolution’s longer available serial time as an advantage.

r005.rationale: It does not identify evolution’s access to real-world data as an advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the most uncertain parameters in the whole model, and I want to be upfront about that. In GATE, the way we handle it is that we don't pick a single number. We specify a distribution over how much effective compute you'd need to train a system that could automate essentially all cognitive tasks in the economy, and then the model propagates that uncertainty through to the outcomes.

The way we anchor the distribution is roughly like this. We start from the compute used for frontier models today, which is somewhere on the order of 10^26, 10^27 FLOP, and then we ask how many more orders of magnitude you'd need on top of that. And there are a few ways to try to get a handle on that. One is biological anchors, the sort of Ajeya Cotra style approach, where you look at the compute the human brain uses over a lifetime, or over evolutionary history, and treat those as reference points. Another is to extrapolate from how capabilities have scaled so far, looking at things like how task horizon length has grown with effective compute, and asking how many more doublings you'd plausibly need. And a third is just to look at the gap between what current systems can do and what full automation requires, and make a judgment call about how large that gap is in terms of the kind of generalization and reliability that's missing.

When you put those together, our median ends up being something like four to six orders of magnitude above where we are now, with a pretty wide tail in both directions. So the distribution puts meaningful probability on it being only a couple of orders of magnitude away, which would mean quite fast timelines, and also meaningful probability on it being eight or more orders of magnitude away, in which case you're really waiting on sustained hardware progress and algorithmic improvements for a long time.

The thing I'd emphasize is that effective compute here means training compute adjusted for algorithmic progress. So it's not just about how many GPUs you buy. If algorithms keep improving at the rate they have been, where you get a few x per year of effective compute gains for free, that compounds and shifts the timeline substantially. In the model, that's one of the main channels, along with the growth in investment and the growth in hardware efficiency.

I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows this number, and the useful thing about putting it in a model like GATE isn't that the median is right, it's that you can see how sensitive everything downstream is to it. And it turns out the economic dynamics, the investment feedback loops, are fairly robust to the exact threshold, while the timing of when you hit full automation is very sensitive to it. So that's where I'd say the real uncertainty lives.

astra-6.text:
I think that’s one of the most uncertain inputs in the model. You’re asking how much effective compute it would take to train a system capable of doing essentially all the tasks that humans do, and we don’t have a direct observation of that threshold.

The distinction between compute and effective compute matters here. Algorithmic improvements can let you get the same capabilities with less physical compute, so the threshold isn’t simply a number of GPUs or a dollar expenditure. It also depends on how efficiently you can use those resources.

You can try to constrain it by looking at what current systems can do and how their capabilities improve with scale. But extrapolating from that to full automation is difficult. A system that can do most tasks might still struggle with a small set of economically important tasks, and those remaining tasks could require substantially more compute—or improvements that scaling alone doesn’t deliver.

So I’d treat this as an uncertain parameter and examine a range of values. The useful question is how much the model’s conclusions change as you move that threshold, rather than whether one particular estimate should be taken literally.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between evolution's computational efficiency and current machine learning.

r005.rationale: It does not mention evolution's access to real-world data as an advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d treat it as one of the biggest uncertainties in the model. Effective compute means compute adjusted for improvements in algorithms, so the question is how much training compute, at some reference level of algorithmic efficiency, would be enough to produce AI that can automate essentially all human work.

We don’t have a direct measurement of that threshold. We can observe how capabilities have improved with scale and try to extrapolate, but there’s a substantial gap between doing well on the tasks we can measure today and being able to do everything that matters economically. Reliability, handling long tasks, and operating in unfamiliar environments could all matter a lot.

So I wouldn’t read a particular setting in GATE as a precise forecast. I’d look at a broad range of possible thresholds and ask how the results change across that range. The model helps us understand the consequences of different assumptions; it doesn’t eliminate the uncertainty about how much compute full automation will actually require.
